guide.name: Guide
guide.welcome: Welcome to Career Plaza. Pick a building. There's no wrong order.
guide.afterFirst: Nice. Your career map just lit up a little. Try another building and notice how it feels different.
guide.afterTwo: You've got enough to look at your growth record. You can keep exploring too.
guide.afterAll: You've been through every building. Skills show up in more than one place, did you notice?

acknowledgements.number: I like that you pointed to a specific figure.
acknowledgements.reason: You gave a reason. That makes it easier to trust.
acknowledgements.question: A good question is a useful tool in this job.
acknowledgements.otherwise: Thanks, that gives me a clear starting point.

scenarios.setting: Client meeting room. A profit chart hangs on the wall.
scenarios.intro: Thanks for jumping in. Our client's profit has fallen 18% this quarter and they want a first view by Friday.
scenarios.question: What would you check first?
scenarios.twist: New info: a competitor cut prices last month.
scenarios.writePrompt: In one or two sentences, what would you tell the client on Friday?
scenarios.invite: It's a chance to see what solving a client's problem under a deadline feels like.

options.text: Break revenue and costs down by product and region to see where the drop is.
options.feedback: That narrows the problem fast. A lot of consultants start there because it turns one big worry into a few smaller ones.
options.twistFeedback: With the price cut in mind, you can check whether the drop sits in the products that compete head to head.
options.reflectiveQuestion: Did sorting through the numbers feel energising or draining?

options.text: Talk to a few of the client's customers about why they're buying less.
options.feedback: Going to the source gives you reasons the numbers can't. It also takes time, which is a real trade-off on a Friday deadline.
options.twistFeedback: Customers may bring up the competitor's price cut, so listen for how much price really drives their choice.
options.reflectiveQuestion: What did you enjoy more: finding the reasons or presenting them?

options.text: Write a one-page summary of what we know and list open questions for the client.
options.feedback: That gets everyone looking at the same picture early. It keeps the client involved instead of surprised.
options.twistFeedback: The competitor's price cut can go at the top of your open questions, so the client sees it straight away.
options.reflectiveQuestion: Would you rather be the person who frames the problem or the one who digs into it?

scenarios.setting: A classroom. Mia is puzzling over her course reading.
scenarios.intro: I read the chapter on social constructivism three times and I still don't get it.
scenarios.question: Could you explain this theory more simply?
scenarios.twist: Mia says she is short on time and has 5 minutes before her next class.
scenarios.writePrompt: Write the first sentence you'd say to Mia.
scenarios.invite: It's a chance to see what explaining ideas feels like as a job.

options.text: Use an everyday example, like how roles get decided in a group project.
options.feedback: Mia's face lights up. Concrete examples help ideas stick, and you picked one she actually lives.
options.twistFeedback: In five minutes, one familiar example is often enough to unlock the idea.
options.reflectiveQuestion: What made you choose that example?

options.text: Break it into three short steps and sketch them on the board.
options.feedback: Clear structure helps when a topic feels like fog. Mia can now see where each idea fits.
options.twistFeedback: Three steps still fit in five minutes if you keep each one to a sentence.
options.reflectiveQuestion: Did planning how to teach it feel more fun than explaining it live?

options.text: Ask what she already understands, then build from there.
options.feedback: You found the gap before explaining. Teachers call this checking prior knowledge.
options.twistFeedback: One quick question fits in five minutes, and it saves time on what she already knows.
options.reflectiveQuestion: How did it feel to lead with a question instead of an answer?

scenarios.setting: An open office. A big dashboard shows user retention.
scenarios.intro: Retention dropped from 42% to 35% over three weeks. The team is asking what's going on.
scenarios.question: How would you investigate it?
scenarios.twist: Leo adds: the drop is mostly new users who signed up through a campus event.
scenarios.writePrompt: Write one hypothesis you'd test first, in a sentence.
scenarios.invite: It's a chance to see how people turn numbers and user stories into decisions.

options.text: Compare retention before and after last month's app update, by user group.
options.feedback: Splitting by group can show whether the drop is everywhere or in one place.
options.twistFeedback: Splitting out the users from the campus event would show their pattern straight away.
options.reflectiveQuestion: How did it feel to work with numbers as evidence?

options.text: Read recent app-store reviews and support tickets.
options.feedback: Real user words give you hypotheses to test. They're messy, but they're often where the story starts.
options.twistFeedback: Look for reviews from people who joined at the campus event. Their first week might tell the story.
options.reflectiveQuestion: Were you more interested in what users said or in what they did?

options.text: Build a timeline of everything that changed in the last month.
options.feedback: A timeline stops the team from blaming the first thing they noticed.
options.twistFeedback: Put the campus event on the timeline and see what else landed that week.
options.reflectiveQuestion: Do you like putting scattered facts into order?

scenarios.setting: A research office. Two reports sit side by side on the desk.
scenarios.intro: Report A says online tutorials improve grades. Report B finds no effect. Both look careful.
scenarios.question: The two sets of results conflict. What would you do?
scenarios.twist: Professor Chen mentions a third report just came out that sides with Report B.
scenarios.writePrompt: In one or two sentences, what would you say to the department about these reports?
scenarios.invite: It's a chance to see what careful, slow investigation feels like day to day.

options.text: Compare their sample sizes, methods and who was studied.
options.feedback: Differences in method often explain differences in results. That's slow, careful work.
options.twistFeedback: The new report gives you a third method to compare. It's fine to update your view as evidence comes in.
options.reflectiveQuestion: Did digging into how the studies were run hold your attention?

options.text: Contact both authors to ask what might explain the gap.
options.feedback: Researchers often respond, and a conversation can surface what the paper left out.
options.twistFeedback: You could ask whether they've seen the new report. Changing your view when the evidence changes is part of the job.
options.reflectiveQuestion: How do you feel about reaching out to people you've never met?

options.text: Write a short note on where the reports agree and where they differ.
options.feedback: Mapping agreement and disagreement gives the next reader a way into both.
options.twistFeedback: Your note can now show two reports on one side. A good summary changes when the evidence does.
options.reflectiveQuestion: Is summarising other people's work something you'd want to do more of?
